subject: Pathology
summary: Atrophy is a decrease in the size of a cell, tissue, or organ. It results from reduced workload, denervation, loss of hormonal stimulation, inadequate nutrition, or aging. Microscopically, it involves shrinkage of cells and often an increase in apoptosis.

sections.p: Atrophy is the irreversible decrease in the size of an organ or tissue due to cell shrinkage. Diagnosis is typically made by clinical examination and confirmed with imaging or biopsy, depending on the affected organ.
b: Characterised by reduced cell size and number.
Can affect any organ or tissue.

t.b: To assess organ size and detect structural changes suggestive of atrophy.
To examine tissue microscopically for cellular shrinkage and loss.

sections.p: Severity is usually described qualitatively as mild, moderate, or severe based on the degree of tissue loss and functional impairment. There are no formal staging systems for general atrophy.
b: Mild atrophy: minimal functional deficit.
Moderate atrophy: noticeable functional impairment.
Severe atrophy: significant loss of function, potentially life-threatening.

sections.p: Causes vary by organ but include disuse, denervation, lack of trophic signals (hormonal or growth factors), inadequate nutrition, and aging. Ischemia can also lead to atrophy.
b: Disuse atrophy (e.g., limb in cast).
Denervation atrophy (e.g., nerve injury).
Hormonal atrophy (e.g., hypopituitarism).
Nutritional deficiency (e.g., severe malnutrition).
Aging (senile atrophy).

sections.p: Presentation depends on the affected organ. It can range from asymptomatic to significant functional decline. For example, muscle atrophy causes weakness, while brain atrophy may lead to cognitive decline.
b: Muscle weakness and reduced bulk.
Cognitive impairment or neurological deficits.
Reduced organ-specific function (e.g., endocrine insufficiency).

sections.p: Investigations are guided by the suspected cause and affected organ. They aim to assess the extent of atrophy and identify underlying pathologies.

t.a: Blood tests (e.g., hormone levels, nutritional markers)
t.b: To identify hormonal deficiencies or nutritional causes.
To measure organ size and detect structural changes.
Microscopic examination of tissue to confirm cellular changes.

sections.p: Severe atrophy can lead to irreversible loss of function. Complications include increased susceptibility to injury, infection, and failure of the affected organ system.
b: Organ failure (e.g., heart failure with cardiac atrophy).
Increased risk of fractures (e.g., osteoporosis).
Severe weakness and immobility.

sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause. If the cause is irreversible or progressive, management aims to slow progression and manage symptoms.
b: Treat underlying cause (e.g., hormone replacement, nutritional support).
Physical therapy and exercise to stimulate muscle or tissue.
Supportive care to manage functional deficits.

sections.p: Follow-up depends on the cause and severity. Prevention involves addressing risk factors like malnutrition, immobility, and hormonal imbalances.
b: Regular monitoring of organ function.
Maintaining adequate nutrition and physical activity.
Addressing hormonal deficiencies promptly.

sections.p: Atrophy can be confused with hypoplasia (underdevelopment) or necrosis (cell death). Functional decline may also mimic other diseases.
b: Hypoplasia: organ is small from development, not shrinkage.
Necrosis: involves cell death, not just shrinkage.
Cachexia: generalised wasting, often due to chronic illness.

sections.p: Imaging may show reduced organ size that is normal for age or due to previous injury rather than active atrophy. Biopsies might miss atrophic areas if sampling is inadequate.
b: Age-related changes can mimic pathological atrophy.
Previous insults may cause permanent size reduction.
Intermittent causes may lead to normal findings between episodes.

faq.a: Mild atrophy, especially if caused by disuse or reversible factors, can sometimes be reversed with appropriate treatment and stimulation.

faq.q: Is atrophy a sign of aging?
faq.a: Some degree of atrophy is a normal part of aging (senile atrophy), but significant atrophy can be caused by various diseases.

faq.q: What is the difference between atrophy and hypertrophy?
faq.a: Atrophy is a decrease in cell size, while hypertrophy is an increase in cell size, usually in response to increased workload.
